blocks.heading: What this section asks you to do
blocks.text: State the reasons governments give for protection, and analyse how each reason runs from the barrier to its consequence.

blocks.heading: Four reasons
blocks.text: Governments give four reasons for protection. The infant industry: a new domestic industry, not yet big enough to produce at the low cost per unit of established rivals, is sheltered until it grows towards that scale. The declining industry: an industry losing ground to cheaper imports is sheltered so the decline is slower, giving workers and equipment time to move. The strategic industry: food, fuel or defence goods are kept going at home so that conflict or shortage abroad cannot cut off the supply. Dumping: where an exporter sells below its cost of production or below its home price to drive rivals out, protection may be used to stop the home market being taken that way.

blocks.heading: The infant-industry chain
blocks.text: The infant-industry argument runs as a chain. A new industry starts small, so its cost per unit tends to sit above established foreign rivals. Protection - a tariff or a quota - raises the import price or caps the import quantity, so home firms keep sales while they grow. As output grows, the cost per unit tends to fall with scale. Where the industry matures, the protection is withdrawn and the industry stands on its own. The caution travels with the argument: where the industry never matures, consumers keep paying the cost of a shelter that has stopped being temporary.

blocks.heading: Dumping, and the other two
blocks.text: The dumping chain runs the same way from a different start. An exporter sells below cost to win the market; home producers lose sales and may close; a tariff or quota raises the dumped price, so home producers keep their market and their workers keep their jobs. The strategic and declining reasons skip the scale argument: their case rests on security in the first and a slower, managed exit in the second, and each is judged by whether the shelter serves that purpose or settles into permanence.

blocks.heading: The declining and strategic industry arguments
blocks.text:
A declining industry is one whose sales are falling for good, often because cheaper imports have taken its market. Without protection it may close suddenly, and where one town depends on it - a clothing mill, a meat-processing plant - the region faces a sharp rise in unemployment. A tariff or quota for a limited period slows the decline, giving workers time to retrain and move to other jobs, and giving the region time to attract new employers. The risk is that the protection stays: consumers keep paying higher prices, and the resources tied up in the industry are not moved to more productive uses.

A strategic industry is one the country needs in a crisis: food, fuel, medicines, power or defence equipment. If the country relied fully on imports, a war, a shortage abroad or an export ban by a supplier could cut supply when it is most needed, as when several countries restricted exports of medical supplies and some foods during the COVID-19 pandemic. Protecting a strategic industry keeps the ability to produce at home, at the cost of higher prices or subsidies in normal times. Namibia's controls on imports of maize and wheat while the local harvest is sold are often defended on these food-security grounds.

blocks.heading: Connections
blocks.text: What these barriers then do to prices, output and jobs at home and abroad is the subject of the next section; the benefits of free trade they give up are those of section 6.2.3.
